newsitem.title: USA: U.S. West Coast crudes sustain gains in late trade.
newsitem.headline: U.S. West Coast crudes sustain gains in late trade.

text.p: U.S. West Coast crude prices sustained morning gains in late trade, rising as West Texas Intermediate (WTI) oil benefitted from lower U.S. crude stocks, traders said.
Data from the American Petroleum Institute (API) showed U.S. crude oil stocks dropped 6.6 million barrels for the week ended November 8.
The draw helped push the benchmark U.S. grade, WTI, up 85 cents on the day, to $23.20/24.30 a barrel; for the December delivery period.
The rise in WTI failed to ignite regional sales of medium-gravity Alaska North Slope (ANS) crude.
The price basis for ANS remained a $2.20 a barrel under December WTI. Earlier in the week the differential tightened after a cargo sold into a West Coast refinery.
BP offered at $1.90 a barrel off December WTI Wednesday, traders said.

West Coast players said they dismissed the API report which showed a five-million-barrel-decrease in the region's supplies. Much of the decrease involves waterborne supplies which are difficult to track, according to traders.
Line 63 crude remained thinly traded in typical early month discussion. The grade, like ANS, rose with higher WTI prices to $21.00/21.30 a barrel.
Arco said it moved up the deadline for Line 63 shippers' nominations to late next week or early next.
Wilmington crude was $17.60/$17.70 a barrel, while Kern River crude stayed $16.15/$16.35 a barrel.
